pages.name: Direction D — matched to your reference

annotations.text:
DIRECTION D — matched to houseofiqf.com

That site is a stock Shopify Dawn theme with photos swapped in. So what you're pointing at isn't a bespoke look — it's the standard Indian D2C register: announcement bar, MRP struck through on every card, trust strip, category tiles, reviews, dark footer.

This is that register, built for womenswear and for single-piece stock. Same conventions, one substitution: where their cards carry a red SALE badge, ours carry a quiet gold "1 piece only" tag.

Earlier directions A–C are on the second page if you want them for comparison.

HOW SCARCITY READS

No countdown on the card. No "only 2 left!", no "14 people viewing". Those are pressure devices, and yours would be true — which makes them worse, not better, because true scarcity stated loudly still reads as a trick.

Instead: a gold tag on the image, and one plain paragraph on the product page saying the piece is also on the rail in the shop.

The 14:38 countdown appears ONLY once a piece is actually held for that shopper. It is information about their own cart, not a nudge.

MOBILE

Majority of your traffic. Sticky buy bar carries the price AND the hold timer, so the countdown stays visible while they scroll the details.

No fake status bar drawn — the real one renders on top.

All tap targets 44px or larger.

TWO THINGS TO DECIDE

1. COD. Your reference offers it, and most Indian D2C does. With single-piece stock it is expensive: a COD order takes the garment off the rail and off the site for the whole delivery round trip, and 20–40% come back refused. Options: no COD; COD above a deposit; or COD only on clearance.

2. Sale badges. The reference discounts everything 30–50% off MRP. Your schema already auto-sets sale price at MRP − 10%, so every piece shows a genuine 10% off. Do you want deeper headline discounts, or is 10% the honest number you want to stand behind?
